Dated this the 13th day of December, 2024 This appeal is filed challenging the order dated 17.07.2024 of the District Judge, Palakkad, in Miscellaneous Application (Arbitration) No.20 of 2024. The said application was filed under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act of 1996") seeking interim measures. Appellant was the petitioner in the said proceedings (hereinafter referred to as "the petitioner") and the respondent herein was the respondent in the M.A.(Arbitration). Brief facts:
2. Petitioner is a partnership firm engaged in civil construction projects whereas, the respondent is a limited liability partnership firm. The petitioner entered into an agreement dated 06.05.2021 with the respondent to construct a slaughterhouse building in the petition- scheduled property. The said agreement contained an arbitration clause. Disputes arose between the parties which later led the respondent to issue a notice rescinding the contract. The petitioner had reasonably been expecting that they would be permitted to carry out and execute the entire work,
but now found itself in a quandary. They apprehend forceful eviction along with their machinery and property which were situated on the work 2024:KER:94296 site and that the respondent may also attempt to alienate the property or complete the work by engaging another contractor. 
Petitioner has already suffered a loss of Rs.1,04,45,000/-. Apprehending further financial loss and damage due to the alleged breach by the respondent, and towards mitigating the same and to secure their interests, the petitioner filed O.P. under Section 9 of the Act of 1996 seeking the following reliefs:
"(a) an order of prohibitory injunction restraining the respondent and their men from forcefully disposing the petitioner and their men from the petition schedule properties ;
(b) an order of prohibitory injunction restraining the respondent and their men from alienating or creating liabilities or encumbering the petition schedule properties and further restraining the respondents and their men from tampering with or effecting any new constructions upon the constructions effected by the petitioner ;" 
Proceedings before the District Court:

2 3. Respondent entered in appearance and filed a counter statement disputing and denying the allegations raised. The execution of the agreement/s and the arbitration clause were admitted. It was inter alia contended that as per the agreement entered into between the parties, the work had to be completed within 240 days (8 months)
and to enable the same, the site had been handed over as early as on 16.11.2021. The 2024:KER:94296 total cost of construction is Rs.9,44,01,797.94 together with GST @
18%. 
A total amount of Rs1,88,80,000/- had been paid including TDS. Petitioner however failed to carry out the work earnestly and the quality of work rendered was also poor. Defects were noted in the work and the petitioner was called upon to rectify the same as it affects the safety of the project. 
However, the petitioner failed to rectify the defects and chose to raise bills quoting exorbitant amounts beyond the terms of the agreement. A total payment of Rs.4,56,45,995/- had already been made to them by the respondent. In view of the breach committed by the petitioner, the respondent rescinded the contract vide letter dated 09.04.2024. A new contractor has been engaged and completion of the balance work has commenced through them. The petitioner is not in possession of the site and hence is not entitled to any injunction as prayed for. The respondent thus prayed for the dismissal of the application.
4. The application under Section 9 had been moved before the Vacation Court (District Court) on 20.04.2024 and in view of a caveat petition filed by the respondent, after hearing the respondent,
the said court had on 23.04.2024 rendered an interim order that the petitioner and their properties should not be removed/evicted from the premises till 29.04.2024. Thereafter based on the interlocutory applications filed by the petitioner from time to time, the interim order was in existence till 01.06.2024. The petitioner also sought to appoint expert Engineers to 2024:KER:94296 evaluate the quality and quantity of work done by them and the same was allowed. 
Two sets of Engineers from the panel submitted by both parties were appointed. Two chartered Engineers, one each from the panel submitted by the parties, filed separate reports. Thereafter the petitioner sought to re-mould the relief of injunction to one for attachment inter alia contending that an amount of Rs.3,47,51,346/- is due to them from the respondent. Based on the pleadings,
three points were raised by the District Court for consideration. Parties were called on to tender evidence. Exts. A1 to A4 were marked from the petitioner's side. 
5. After hearing both sides, the District Court rendered an order dismissing the petition inter alia holding that the petitioner was not entitled to injunction as sought for. The District Court reasoned that since the agreement already stood terminated and the work had been assigned to another contractor, there was no reason for the petitioner or their machinery and material to remain at the work site. Further, since the reports of the experts after due inspection have already been filed and are available on record, the interests of the petitioner stands protected and there is no reason to sustain the prayer for injunction. As regards the amendment sought to enable a prayer for attachment, the same was not granted inter alia pointing out that by the very nature of the relief and the valuation stated in the petition, prayer for attachment can be maintained only before the competent court having jurisdiction viz., the Commercial 2024:KER:94296 Court. The said order dated 17.07.2024 of the District Court dismissing the M.A.(Arbitration) is challenged in this appeal.

3 6. Heard Sri.Firoz K.M. learned counsel appearing for the petitioner and Sri.P.K.Sajeev, learned counsel appearing for the respondent.
Contentions in brief:
7. The principal contention put forth by the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner is that if the District Court found that it lacked jurisdiction, it ought to have returned the petition to enable presentation before the proper forum rather than answering the prayers sought on merits. The petition had been moved before a Vacation Court and at that point in time, the District Court as per the relevant provision in the Kerala Civil Courts Act, 1957 was the competent court wherein the petition could be filed. After the grant of interim prayer, had the petitioner been relegated to the proper court, they would have pursued their remedies in the proper forum. The said option which was otherwise available now stands foreclosed by the order on merits passed by the District Court. 
Since the order under challenge touches upon the merits of the matter and the contentions raised,
the same would stare upon the petitioner even if a competent court having jurisdiction is moved with the same reliefs. Further, pointing to Section 2 (1) (c) (iv) and Section 10 of the Commercial Courts Act 2015, it is contended that disputes arising from 2024:KER:94296 constructions or infrastructure contracts of specified value, fall within the definition of commercial disputes and hence could only be the subject matter of the jurisdiction of Commercial Courts and not that of the District Court. The remedy by way of injunctions which was granted by the District Court till the work was assessed by the competent Engineers does not fully protect the interests of the petitioner. 
A further assessment of the work and materials is even now necessary and an attachment of the property is also needed to secure an amount to the tune of Rs.3,47,51,346/-. The counsel thus seeks to set aside the order impugned and prays for a direction to the District Court to transfer Section 9 petition to the competent Commercial Court or to return the same to the petitioner for presentation before the competent Commercial Court. It is also submitted that subsequent to the rendering of the impugned order, the petitioner had moved this Court with an Arbitration Request, and this Court has already allowed the same and has appointed an arbitrator. Thus now confronted with the bar as laid down in Section 9 (3) of the Act of 1996, the learned counsel contends that the same is not a total bar and if the court finds that circumstances exist that may not render the remedy provided under Section 17 to be 'efficacious', interim measures could be granted by the Court even though an arbitrator has already been appointed. The learned counsel thus seeks a direction to set aside the impugned order of the District Court and to enable the petitioner to move 2024:KER:94296 the competent Commercial Court seeking further interim measures prior to the commencement of the arbitration proceedings. 
8. Per contra, the learned counsel for the respondent submits that the District Court has not erred in rendering the impugned order. He refutes the contention that the court did not have jurisdiction to entertain the matter and terms it as misplaced and a clear afterthought. He submits that the said contention as to jurisdiction is put forth overlooking the fact that in the order it relates only to the subsequent prayer for an attachment which was later sought to be incorporated by way of amending the petition. The District Court had validly adjudicated the petition which was filed in the Vacation Court invoking Section 9 of the Act of 1996 seeking injunctions as interim measures. The same had been entertained by the Court and an interim order was granted in favour of the Petitioner which C-Disc Technologies Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Meatin Farms And Foods Llp on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/99040644/
4 was being extended by the petitioner from time to time. The I.As. subsequently filed by the petitioner were also entertained by the District Court and the petitioner acquiesced to the jurisdiction thus exercised. Further at the instance of the petitioner, an expert panel of chartered Engineers visited the site and submitted reports. Thus all the concerns of the petitioner at the time of filing the petition had been met with the orders issued and their interests prior to the initiation of the arbitration proceedings had been fully protected. It is in this background that the amended prayer for attachment sought to be made was denied by the 2024:KER:94296 District Court holding that the same lay beyond its jurisdiction. The contentions raised in this appeal are not further unsustainable in view of the fact that the petitioner themselves had moved this Court for the appointment of an arbitrator and the said petition has been allowed and an arbitrator has been appointed. It is trite law that once an arbitral tribunal is constituted, the court shall not entertain an application under sub-section (1) of Section 9 of the Act of 1996. Hence the prayer now made to set aside the order of the District Judge, so as to enable the petitioner to move the competent Commercial Court seeking interim measures is unsustainable in law. He thus seeks a dismissal of the Arb. Appeal. 
Discussion and findings:
9. It is admitted by both sides that subsequent to the rendering of the impugned order, the petitioner had moved this Court with an Arbitration Request (A.R. No.125 of 2024), which was disposed of by this Court vide order dated 14.10.2024 appointing a sole arbitrator. Thus as on date,
an arbitrator has already been appointed to adjudicate and resolve the disputes and differences between the petitioner and the respondent. This aspect has to be borne in mind while proceeding to consider the contentions raised by both sides. 
10. The petition invoking Section 9 of the Act of 1996 was originally filed seeking injunctions on two counts. The first injunction was 2024:KER:94296 sought to restrain the respondent from forcibly disposing the petitioner and their men from the petition-scheduled properties. The second prayer was to injunct the respondent from alienating or encumbering the petition schedule properties and to restrain them from tampering with or adding on to the civil works already completed by the petitioner. Thus the objective of the petitioner was to protect his interests in the forthcoming arbitration proceedings by way of interim measures, lest the respondent changes or tampers with the work already done or alienates or endangers the machinery and material of the petitioner at the site. Interim orders were initially granted by the District Court (the Vacation Court at the relevant time) and the respondent was restrained from obstructing the work carried on by the petitioner. 
Thereafter expert Engineers appointed by the court inspected the work site and submitted detailed reports. The interim orders granted were being extended from time to time till the expert team filed their report. Once the reports had been filed and the assessment of work done by the petitioner had been duly recorded, the interim order was not further required to be extended and the same had expired. No relief for recovery of any amounts or for attachment of property had been sought in the petition originally. The interim injunctions sought, as stated above, were for the limited purpose of securing interests of the petitioner pending the initiation of arbitration proceedings. Since the agreement with the petitioner stood rescinded, new contractors were appointed by the 2024:KER:94296 respondent to pursue the work further. Petitioner hence had no reason to remain C-Disc Technologies Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Meatin Farms And Foods Llp on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/99040644/
5 in the petition schedule property. The reports already submitted by the teams of expert Engineers have already recorded the factual details needed to safeguard the contentions of the petitioner regarding the nature, extent, quantity, and quality of the work already carried out by the petitioner. 
The said reports thus secure the evidence, if any, needed for sustaining the petitioner's proposed monetary claim in the arbitration proceedings. It is thereafter that the petitioner chose to seek a modification of the relief by adding a prayer for attachment of the petition schedule properties and for a direction to the respondent to furnish security to the tune of Rs.3,47,51,346/-.
11. The said prayer for an amendment to include relief of attachment and security was declined by the District Court on the very same day of dismissal of the M.A.(Arb.). Three reasons have been stated in the order impugned. Firstly, in the entire petition, there was no apprehension that the respondent was attempting to alienate the property to defeat or delay the reliefs which the petitioner is entitled to in the arbitration proceedings. The only apprehension was that if the quantity and quality of work done by the petitioner were not recorded and the property was alienated, the petitioner would be put to irreparable injury and loss. None of the ingredients for seeking an attachment had been pleaded. Secondly, the work at the site after rescinding of the agreement 2024:KER:94296 with the petitioner had already been re-commenced by another contractor which revealed that the respondent had no intention to alienate the property and was only proceeding to complete the work of the slaughterhouse. Thirdly it was stated that since the petitioner is now seeking to amend the petition and attach the property and furnish security claiming entitlement to more than Rs.2,43,08,346/-, the District Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the attachment and security plea since the pecuniary jurisdiction had been exceeded. The sum and substance of the finding of the District Court is thus that a petitioner who had sought interim measures and had obtained favourable orders securing his interests, cannot later vary the reliefs sought as to place the matter beyond the jurisdiction limits of the court wherein it had been pending and then seek for transfer the matter to a court having jurisdiction. 
12. In the appeal, the third portion of the order has been highlighted by the petitioner as the principal ground for challenging the order of the District Court. It is contended that once jurisdiction has been found to be non-existent, the Court ought not have proceeded on answer on merits. This contention put forth by the petitioner cannot be sustained in the facts and circumstances of the case. The interim measures originally sought by the petitioner had already been granted by the District Court. The interests of the petitioner thus stood secured. The petitioner had thereafter sought to amend the petition and include a new prayer of 2024:KER:94296 attachment which was declined by the District Court vide impugned order. Subsequently, at the instance of the petitioner, an arbitrator was appointed by this Court vide order dated 14.10.2024. 
Petitioner had thereafter filed the above appeal on 17.10.2024 seeking to set aside the order of the District Court and seeking to transfer the petition to a Commercial Court. The learned District Judge has in the impugned order stated that after obtaining an interim injunction as early as on 23.05.2023, it is not deemed proper to return the petition for presentation before the Commercial Court. The said finding of the learned Judge, in the facts of the case, cannot be found fault with or termed as incorrect. 
C-Disc Technologies Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Meatin Farms And Foods Llp on 13 December, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/99040644/
6 13. Moreover, the fact that this Court has already appointed a sole arbitrator to arbitrate on the dispute between the petitioner and the respondent makes the petitioner's prayer in the appeal unsustainable. Entertaining a prayer for interim measures by a court subsequent to the appointment of an arbitrator is hit by the express bar provided in Section 9(3) of the Act of 1996. The legislative object and intent behind such a provision is to channel the interim reliefs that the parties may seek after the appointment of an arbitrator, through the arbitrator thus appointed. Parties in such cases can invoke Section 17 of the Act of 1996 which stipulates the interim measures that could be ordered by the Arbitral Tribunal. They cannot generally revert back to the court with an application under Section 9(1). However, there is indeed an exception to 2024:KER:94296 the prohibition envisaged and it is found in Section 9(3). The same comes into play when the court finds that circumstances do exist that may not render the remedy provided under Section 17 (interim measures ordered by the Tribunal) efficacious. In such circumstances, the court may be justified in entertaining the application under Section 9(1) even after the appointment of an arbitrator. The learned counsel for the petitioner has vehemently argued that since the prohibition under Section 9(3) is not absolute and since its last limb stipulates an exception, the petitioner is entitled to seek the Section 9(1)
application, to be transferred, albeit after its disposal, to the competent Commercial Court so that the said court could ascertain whether such circumstances as envisaged under the last limb of Section 9(3) exists justifying it to be entertained. This prayer of the learned counsel cannot be granted for more reasons than one. Firstly, the petitioner had moved an application under Section 9(1) and has already obtained interim measures that were deemed necessary to protect their interests at the relevant point of time. Through the said interim orders obtained, the immediate and primary concerns of the petitioner, already stand addressed. Thereafter the said Section 9(1)
application, stands closed vide the impugned order. It is subsequent thereto, that the arbitrator has been appointed by this Court to arbitrate the subject dispute. Hence any further interim measures that the petitioner is desirous of obtaining can be sought before the arbitrator invoking Section 17. 
The 2024:KER:94296 contention that the court which the petitioner had moved earlier under Section 9(1) and obtained certain interim measures was not the proper court and had no jurisdiction to entertain the application cannot be sustained at this point of time that too based on an amendment petition. It is also relevant to note that the exception to the bar of courts entertaining an application under Section 9 (3) generally envisages situations where the arbitrator has been appointed while the application for interim measures etc. under Section 9 (1) is pending or is in consideration before the court. Once the proceedings under Section 9 (1) have culminated and subsequently an arbitrator has been appointed, ordinarily, all further prayers of interim measures,
except the ones that may fall in the last limb of Section 9 (3) are to be raised before the arbitrator so appointed. 
In view of the above, I do not see any reason to interfere with the order impugned. This appeal fails and it is dismissed. No costs.

Entertaining a prayer for interim measures by a court subsequent to the appointment of an arbitrator is hit by the express bar provided in Section 9(3) of the Act of 1996.
The legislative object and intent behind such a provision is to channel the interim reliefs that the parties may seek after the appointment of an arbitrator, through the arbitrator thus appointed.
Parties in such cases can invoke Section 17 of the Act of 1996 which stipulates the interim measures that could be ordered by the Arbitral Tribunal.
They cannot generally revert back to the court with an application under Section 9(1).
However, there is indeed an exception to 2024:KER:94296 the prohibition envisaged and it is found in Section 9(3).
The same comes into play when the court finds that circumstances do exist that may not render the remedy provided under Section 17 (interim measures ordered by the Tribunal) efficacious.
In such circumstances, the court may be justified in entertaining the application under Section 9(1) even after the appointment of an arbitrator.

The learned counsel for the petitioner has vehemently argued that since the prohibition under Section 9(3) is not absolute and since its last limb stipulates an exception, the petitioner is entitled to seek the Section 9(1)
application, to be transferred, albeit after its disposal, to the competent Commercial Court so that the said court could ascertain whether such circumstances as envisaged under the last limb of Section 9(3) exists justifying it to be entertained.
This prayer of the learned counsel cannot be granted for more reasons than one.

application, stands closed vide the impugned order.
It is subsequent thereto, that the arbitrator has been appointed by this Court to arbitrate the subject dispute.
Hence any further interim measures that the petitioner is desirous of obtaining can be sought before the arbitrator invoking Section 17.

The 2024:KER:94296 contention that the court which the petitioner had moved earlier under Section 9(1) and obtained certain interim measures was not the proper court and had no jurisdiction to entertain the application cannot be sustained at this point of time that too based on an amendment petition.

It is also relevant to note that the exception to the bar of courts entertaining an application under Section 9 (3) generally envisages situations where the arbitrator has been appointed while the application for interim measures etc. under Section 9 (1) is pending or is in consideration before the court.

Once the proceedings under Section 9 (1) have culminated and subsequently an arbitrator has been appointed, ordinarily, all further prayers of interim measures,
except the ones that may fall in the last limb of Section 9 (3) are to be raised before the arbitrator so appointed.
In view of the above, I do not see any reason to interfere with the order impugned.
